column5: righteous and wicked ways
column6: The commentary says the requested road is recognized by its travelers; Psalm 1:6 says YHWH knows the righteous way while the wicked way perishes, making the walkers and their endpoint distinguish the two paths.

column5: shepherd leads on righteous paths
column6: The commentary reads the straight road as a lived route shaped by its company; Psalm 23:3 has the shepherd restore the speaker and lead him on paths of righteousness, so guidance is personal and ongoing.

column5: Abraham's household keeps YHWH's way
column6: The commentary says the blessed path is practiced, not inherited automatically; Genesis 18:19 says Abraham is chosen so his household and descendants keep YHWH's way by doing righteousness and justice.

column5: choose life or death, blessing or curse
column6: The commentary distinguishes the blessed from wrath-struck and straying groups without making status hereditary; Deuteronomy sets life and death, blessing and curse before Israel and urges a choice, tying destination to response.

column5: one bears one's own guilt
column6: The commentary says the road belongs to those who walk it, not to a blessed person's descendants by birth; Ezekiel says neither son nor father bears the other's guilt, locating judgment in each person's own conduct.

column5: the wicked can turn and live
column6: The commentary treats straying as a state from which a person may return; Ezekiel says a wicked person who turns from sin and keeps justice will live, making the path recoverable.

column5: the righteous can turn away
column6: The commentary refuses to make the blessed road an inherited, permanent label; Ezekiel also says a formerly righteous person who turns to wrongdoing will die, so past standing does not replace present walking.

column5: God leads Israel through the wilderness
column6: The commentary calls the requested road an everyday route with a guide and fellow travelers; Exodus depicts YHWH going before Israel in cloud and fire to lead them on their journey, grounding the image in a people led together.

column5: the whole wilderness way
column6: The commentary treats guidance as a path actually walked and tested; Deuteronomy asks Israel to remember the whole way YHWH led them for forty years, adding that the road forms the travelers as it brings them onward.

column5: nations learn and walk God's paths
column6: The commentary says the path is identified by the people who walk it; Isaiah has many peoples invite one another to learn God's ways and walk in his paths, turning guidance into a shared, imitable course.

column5: voice says which way to walk
column6: The commentary distinguishes a guided route from wandering; Isaiah 30:21 pictures a voice behind the hearer directing, “This is the way; walk in it,” when the hearer turns right or left.

column5: wanderers led on a straight way
column6: The commentary contrasts lost wandering with a road that reaches its destination; Psalm 107:7 says God led the wanderers on a straight way to an inhabited city, joining guidance to arrival and shelter.

column5: righteous path brightens
column6: The commentary distinguishes the straight path from straying by how its travelers proceed; Proverbs 4:18 compares the righteous path to dawn light growing brighter, giving the good road a visible direction.

column5: wicked stumble in darkness
column6: The commentary says straying is a journey without a clear way; Proverbs 4:19 says the wicked way is darkness and its travelers do not know what makes them stumble.

column5: holy highway for the redeemed
column6: The commentary insists that a road is defined by its destination and travelers; Isaiah describes a highway called holy on which the redeemed walk, with the unclean excluded, making holiness a quality of the company and course.

column5: God leads the blind on an unknown road
column6: The commentary's straying image includes not knowing where one goes; Isaiah promises to lead the blind by an unfamiliar way, turn darkness to light, and not forsake them, so lostness can be met by divine guidance.

column5: each sheep turns to its own way
column6: The commentary contrasts a shared road with paths lost by following the wrong company; Isaiah says all have gone astray like sheep, each turning to his own way, giving the collective image of dispersed travelers a moral edge.

column5: seek the good old way
column6: The commentary describes a route inherited through the footprints of earlier walkers; Jeremiah calls the people to ask for the ancient paths, find the good way, and walk in it, while the verse records their refusal.

column5: prayer to be led on level ground
column6: The commentary reads the ayah as a direct request for guidance into the path of God's favored people; the psalmist asks God to teach his will and have the good spirit lead him on level ground, making the route itself a prayer.

column5: lost sheep asks to be sought
column6: The commentary keeps the lost traveler distinct from the guide and the destination; Psalm 119:176 calls the speaker a lost sheep and asks God to seek him, adding that straying need not be the final identity.

column5: Ruth chooses Naomi's people and God
column6: The commentary says the road's companions are joined by faithful walking rather than automatic descent; Ruth, a foreign widow, binds herself to Naomi's people and God, showing chosen belonging through shared life.

column5: choice between following YHWH and Baal
column6: The commentary separates two opposed paths with a renewed negation; Elijah asks Israel how long it will limp between two opinions and tells them to follow whichever god is truly God, making divided allegiance a concrete fork in the road.

column5: confession of having left truth's way
column6: The commentary contrasts a road that reaches its goal with straying into loss; the condemned in Wisdom 5 confess that they left the way of truth, missed righteousness's light, and traveled trackless paths, turning the image into a retrospective confession.

column5: narrow route between fire and deep water
column6: The commentary explicitly treats the straight path as lived conduct rather than a hair-thin bridge; 4 Ezra pictures the desired city as an inheritance reached by one path between fire and deep water, a distinct Jewish afterlife image that contrasts with the daily road described here.

column5: Torah is not an inheritance
column6: The commentary says descendants do not inherit the blessed path without walking it; Avot tells the learner to prepare for Torah because it is not an inheritance, making study and practice rather than ancestry the condition of belonging.

column5: Noah walks with God, Abraham before God
column6: The commentary makes following earlier walkers the way into the path; Genesis Rabbah interprets “walked with God” of Noah as needing support, but “walk before me” of Abraham as strength, changing the parallel into two forms of guided walking.

column5: feet guided into the way of peace
column6: The commentary asks for guidance into a road walked by people; Luke's song says the dawn from on high will guide our feet into the way of peace and shine on those in darkness, joining guided steps to rescue from lostness.

column5: followers walk in light, not darkness
column6: The commentary contrasts the guided road with wandering; Jesus says the one who follows him will not walk in darkness but have the light of life, explicitly tying a person's path to whom they follow.

column5: sheep follow the shepherd's voice
column6: The commentary says the path is known by its walkers and their guide; John depicts the shepherd going ahead and the sheep following because they know his voice, making guidance a relationship shared by a flock.

column5: narrow way leads to life
column6: The commentary says the Qur'anic road is ordinary lived conduct, not a trial bridge; Matthew's narrow road leads to life and is found by few, a close two-path comparison that also preserves a different emphasis on entry and destination.

column5: blessed inherit the kingdom at judgment
column6: The commentary names those receiving God's favor and sets them apart from the wrath-struck and straying; at judgment the Son of Man calls the sheep blessed by his Father and invites them to inherit the kingdom, linking blessing to an eschatological company.

column5: cursed sent away at judgment
column6: The commentary distinguishes the blessed from those under wrath; Matthew has the King send the goats away as cursed, supplying a judgment scene with a sharply separated opposite company.

column5: Abraham's descent is no guarantee
column6: The commentary says the path does not pass automatically from blessed ancestors to descendants; John warns his hearers not to rely on “We have Abraham as father,” since God can raise Abraham's children from stones, shifting status to repentance and fruit.

column5: Abraham's children do Abraham's works
column6: The commentary says the blessed road belongs to those who walk as earlier figures walked; Jesus says Abraham's true children would do Abraham's works, making kinship a matter of imitation rather than ancestry alone.

column5: Abraham's children walk in his faith's footsteps
column6: The commentary describes a road as the trace left by its earlier travelers; Paul identifies Abraham's family with those who walk in the footsteps of the faith Abraham had, an unusually close formulation of the path's companions.

column5: shepherd seeks the lost sheep
column6: The commentary's last group can be anyone who loses the way, and its camel image is a separated animal; Jesus' shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to seek one lost sheep, showing that the straying traveler remains sought and valued.

column5: straying sheep return to their shepherd
column6: The commentary holds straying and return together rather than treating the lost as a fixed people; Peter says his hearers were like sheep going astray but have returned to the shepherd and guardian of their souls.

column5: two ways, life and death
column6: The commentary separates the guided road from straying and asks the reader to recognize their travelers; the Didache opens with two ways, one of life and one of death, then distinguishes them by concrete conduct.

column5: two ways of light and darkness
column6: The commentary sets the blessed path against distinct forms of ruin; Barnabas introduces two ways, light and darkness, and says their governing powers and travelers differ, offering an early Christian ethical map alongside the Qur'anic prayer.

column5: God finds and guards Israel in the wilderness
column6: The commentary's image of lostness includes a traveler without a known route; Deuteronomy says God found Israel in a desert waste, guarded him, and cared for him, supplying a scriptural scene of the lost being gathered into God's care.

column5: Hebrew no'am, pleasantness
column6: The commentary labels anʿamta with Arabic root n-ʿ-m and develops softness, ease, and favor as nearby resonances; Hebrew no'am in Psalm 90:17 asks that the Lord's pleasant favor rest on his servants and establish their work, a cognate echo without equating the senses.

column5: disciples of Abraham and Balaam
column6: The commentary identifies the road by the character of its travelers; Avot distinguishes Abraham's disciples from Balaam's by their eye, spirit, and soul, so following a patriarch is ethical imitation rather than mere descent.

column5: repentant can rise beyond the righteous
column6: The commentary says a straying person may return to the guided path; Berakhot teaches that penitents stand where the completely righteous cannot, giving rabbinic weight to movement between the categories.

column5: outsiders join the patriarchs' table
column6: The commentary says the path's company is not inherited by blood; Jesus says people will come from east and west, north and south to dine in God's kingdom, while others claiming place are excluded, unsettling inherited privilege.

column5: people of faith are Abraham's children
column6: The commentary makes the way of the blessed a path that can be joined by walking it; Paul calls those of faith Abraham's children, extending kinship by allegiance rather than genealogy.

column5: followers are called the Way
column6: The commentary says the road is recognized by the people who walk it; Acts describes the Damascus believers as belonging to “the Way,” showing a Christian community named by its shared route.
